title: IF SEX MAKES TWO PEOPLE “ONE FLESH”… WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THERE’S A THIRD?
paragraphs:
IF SEX MAKES TWO PEOPLE “ONE FLESH”… WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THERE’S A THIRD?
What adultery, sexual history, multiple partners, and polygamy reveal about one of the Bible’s most misunderstood—and painfully personal—truths
There is a question Christians sometimes whisper because saying it out loud feels dangerous.
If sex makes two people “one flesh”…
what happens when one of them sleeps with somebody else?
Does that person now become “one flesh” with two people?
What if there have been ten partners?
What about someone who lived promiscuously before coming to Christ?
What about adultery?
And perhaps the question that makes everything even more uncomfortable:
What about the men in the Bible who had multiple wives?
If “one flesh” means what Christians often say it means, how does any of this fit together?
Stay with me, because somewhere inside this question is something much bigger than sex.
It is about covenant.
It is about betrayal.
It is about why sexual sin can hurt so deeply.
It is about why God designed marriage the way He did.
And ultimately, it is about whether your past can still follow you after Jesus has called you His.
We have to begin where Scripture begins.
Before adultery.
Before pornography.
Before broken marriages.
Before Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon, or any of the complicated relationships that followed.
There was a garden.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 says in Hebrew:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzāḇ-’îš ’eṯ-’āḇîw wə’eṯ-’immô, wəḏāḇaq bə’ištô; wəhāyû ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ.
In straightforward English:
“Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.”
Look carefully.
There is movement in the verse.
He leaves.
He clings.
They become.
The Hebrew verb דָּבַק — dābaq — carries the idea of clinging, adhering, holding fast.
And then comes the phrase that has echoed through thousands of years:
בָשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad.
“One flesh.”
The Bible does not introduce sex as merely two bodies experiencing pleasure.
God places sexual union inside something larger: the covenantal union of husband and wife.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because years later, Jesus reaches all the way back to this creation account when people question Him about marriage.
He does not begin with whatever human beings had normalized.
He goes back to creation.
He speaks of the Creator making them male and female, of a man leaving father and mother and being joined to his wife, and of the two becoming one flesh.
Then Jesus draws the conclusion:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Notice where Christ takes us.
Back to God’s design.
Not merely sexual chemistry.
Not merely attraction.
Not merely desire.
God joining husband and wife in a union that human beings are not supposed to tear apart.
But now we reach the uncomfortable part.
Because Paul says something in 1 Corinthians 6 that prevents us from treating sex casually even outside marriage.
He is warning Christians about sexual immorality, and specifically about intercourse with a prostitute.
And Paul writes:
ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν; Ἔσονται γάρ, φησίν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.
The shocking point is essentially this:
Do you not know that the person joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, Scripture says, “the two will become one flesh.”
Read that again.
Paul takes language rooted in Genesis and applies it to an immoral sexual encounter.
That destroys one popular Christian oversimplification.
You sometimes hear:
“Sex makes you married in God’s eyes.”
But Paul does not call the prostitute the man’s wife.
He tells the man to flee sexual immorality.
If intercourse automatically constituted a complete biblical marriage covenant, Paul’s argument would become extraordinarily strange.
Instead, Scripture gives us a more careful—and more sobering—picture.
Sex does not appear to be identical to marriage.
But sex is profoundly connected to the one-flesh reality for which marriage was designed.
That is why casual sex is not actually casual in biblical theology.
The body participates in something that was designed to speak the language of covenant even when the people involved refuse the covenant surrounding it.
Think about that.
The body can say something the heart refuses to promise.
“I give myself to you.”
And then morning comes.
One person gets dressed.
Someone checks a phone.
Someone says, “Last night was fun.”
And two people walk away pretending nothing profound happened.
But Scripture refuses to make sex that small.
Paul’s Greek word for being “joined” in 1 Corinthians 6:16 is κολλώμενος — kollōmenos, from kollaō, language associated with joining or adhering.
This is why Paul does not say:
“It doesn't matter. It was only physical.”
He argues almost exactly the opposite.
Your body matters.
And immediately after discussing sexual immorality, Paul reminds believers that their bodies belong to Christ and are temples of the Holy Spirit.
Christian sexual ethics therefore does not begin with God hating pleasure.
It begins with God assigning extraordinary dignity to the human body.
Your body matters because you matter.
And sex matters because God designed it to unite persons in a way that is meant to belong inside covenant faithfulness.
So what happens when someone has sex with another person?
According to Paul, something genuinely bodily and morally significant happens.
A one-body, one-flesh reality is involved.
But that does not mean every sexual partner becomes another permanent spouse in some invisible heavenly marriage registry.
Scripture never tells sexually immoral converts that they must locate every previous sexual partner and treat each person as a continuing spouse.
Instead, Scripture tells sinners something far more powerful:
Repent.
Flee sexual immorality.
Belong to Christ.
And this becomes breathtaking when we remember whom Paul was addressing.
Immediately before this discussion, Paul lists serious sins from which members of the Corinthian church had come.
Then come three of the most beautiful words ever spoken over a ruined past:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Past tense.
Something happened.
They were washed.
They were sanctified.
They were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Do you understand what that means for the person reading this who has been silently counting?
Two partners.
Five.
Twenty.
Maybe you cannot remember.
Maybe you can remember every face.
Maybe your sin was adultery.
Maybe someone committed adultery against you.
Maybe pornography rewired your expectations of intimacy.
Maybe somebody used your body and disappeared.
Maybe you willingly participated in things you now deeply regret.
Maybe you were sexually sinned against—and this distinction is essential: what someone did to you without your consent is not your sexual sin. The shame belongs to the offender, not the victim.
And maybe the hardest person for you to forgive is the person you used to be.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross only for people with clean histories.
The Gospel is not:
“Jesus saves everyone except people who made sexual mistakes.”
The Gospel is that sinners can be washed.
Not excused.
Washed.
Not told that sin was harmless.
Forgiven.
Not told that rebellion did not matter.
Redeemed.
Grace does not need to pretend sin was small in order to prove that Christ is greater.
That brings us to adultery.
What happens when a married person sleeps with someone else?
They do not somehow become “half married” to two people.
Rather, adultery takes something designed to express exclusive marital union and directs it toward someone outside that covenant.
That is part of why betrayal can feel almost physical to the betrayed spouse.
Something that belonged inside the exclusivity of the marriage was given elsewhere.
The marriage covenant has been violated.
One-flesh sexuality has been taken outside the covenant where God intended it to flourish.
Jesus treats adultery seriously precisely because marriage is serious.
But even here we must never preach condemnation more loudly than the cross.
Adultery can destroy trust.
It can devastate families.
It can produce consequences that forgiveness does not instantly erase.
Repentance does not mean pretending damage never happened.
Reconciliation may require confession, truth, accountability, changed behavior, rebuilding trust, pastoral wisdom, and time.
But adultery is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
There are people reading this who desperately need that sentence.
Adultery is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Sexual immorality is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Pornography is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Your past is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Now we come to polygamy.
Someone will immediately say:
“But Abraham had more than one woman.”
“Jacob had Leah and Rachel.”
“David had multiple wives.”
“Solomon had hundreds.”
Yes.
The Bible records polygamy.
But recording something is not the same as prescribing it.
That distinction protects us from terrible theology.
Scripture records murder.
Scripture records deception.
Scripture records incest.
Scripture records idolatry.
Narrative description does not automatically equal divine endorsement.
Even Israel’s law recognizes situations in which a man has two wives and regulates inheritance rights so that favoritism does not deprive the rightful firstborn.
That legislation shows that Scripture addresses polygamous realities within fallen human society.
But regulation of a broken situation is not the same thing as establishing that situation as the creation ideal.
And what is fascinating is what repeatedly happens when polygamy appears in biblical narratives.
Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar?
Pain.
Jacob, Leah, and Rachel?
Rivalry.
Hannah and Peninnah?
Provocation and grief.
Solomon’s many wives?
His heart is eventually turned toward other gods.
The Bible hardly needs to interrupt every story and shout, “THIS IS COMPLICATED.”
The stories themselves bleed.
And when Jesus is asked about marriage, He does something decisive.
He returns to the beginning.
One man.
His wife.
The two.
One flesh.
Jesus does not build His theology of marriage from Solomon’s palace.
He builds it from Eden.
That is enormously important.
We should not allow humanity’s later arrangements to redefine God’s original pattern.
Yet there is another danger here.
Some Christians become fascinated with whether previous partners create mysterious “soul ties” that must be individually broken through special formulas or rituals.
We should be careful.
The Bible absolutely treats sexual union as spiritually and morally serious.
Paul unquestionably uses Genesis one-flesh language in discussing prostitution.
But Scripture does not give Christians an elaborate doctrine requiring special “soul-tie breaking” ceremonies for every previous sexual partner.
Our confidence must rest somewhere much stronger.
Christ.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Sanctification.
The indwelling Holy Spirit.
The authority of Jesus Christ over the believer’s life.
You do not need to invent a ritual stronger than the Gospel.
You need Jesus.
And maybe that is where this entire conversation was always heading.
Because perhaps you clicked this article expecting an argument about sex.
Instead, Scripture has been quietly asking:
Who owns you now?
Your past?
Your desires?
Your wounds?
Your spouse?
Your former partners?
Your shame?
Or Christ?
Paul’s answer is astonishing.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
Your body.
The body that sinned.
The body that was hurt.
The body that remembers.
The body you sometimes hate.
The body you sometimes used for validation because you desperately wanted somebody to tell you that you were desirable.
That body can now glorify God.
Maybe nobody ever explained holiness to you this way.
Holiness is not God saying:
“Your body is disgusting.”
Holiness is God saying:
“Your body is too valuable to surrender to everything that wants access to it.”
There is a difference.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been living divided.
Church on Sunday.
Secret messages Monday night.
Worship music playing while pornography remains hidden in another tab.
A wedding ring on the hand while another person lives in the imagination.
A Bible beside the bed where somebody who is not your spouse sometimes sleeps.
Nobody knows.
Except you.
And God.
Maybe this is the moment you stop hiding.
Not because Christians are supposed to pretend temptation disappears.
But because Jesus did not die so that we could decorate our chains with Bible verses.
He came to set captives free.
Repentance means turning.
Sometimes trembling.
Sometimes crying.
Sometimes deleting a number.
Sometimes confessing what pride desperately wants hidden.
Sometimes installing accountability.
Sometimes ending a relationship you already know dishonors Christ.
Sometimes finally telling a trusted mature Christian, pastor, counselor, or spouse the truth that secrecy has been feeding.
But repentance does not walk toward punishment hoping God might eventually become merciful.
Repentance runs toward the God whose mercy is already calling the sinner home.
That is the scandal.
We sinned.
He pursued.
We hid.
He called.
We wandered.
He came looking.
We carried shame.
He carried a cross.
And when Christ stretched out His hands at Calvary, He did not say:
“Clean yourself up and then come back.”
He paid for sinners who could never make themselves clean enough.
That is why the Christian story can never end with sexual failure.
The final word belongs to Jesus.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe your history is complicated.
Maybe you are single and tired of waiting.
Maybe you crossed boundaries last night.
Maybe your spouse does not know what you have done.
Maybe you have remained sexually faithful but secretly carry arrogance toward people whose stories are messier than yours.
Then every one of us needs the same Savior.
The sexually broken need Jesus.
The sexually proud need Jesus.
The adulterer needs Jesus.
The betrayed spouse needs Jesus.
The virgin needs Jesus.
The person with fifty former partners needs Jesus.
The person who has never kissed anyone needs Jesus.
Nobody enters the Kingdom because his or her sexual résumé was impressive.
We enter through Christ.
And Christ does not merely forgive.
He transforms.
So yes, sex creates a profound one-flesh bodily union.
Yes, sexual activity outside marriage takes something God designed for covenant and tears it away from its intended home.
Yes, adultery violates marital exclusivity.
Yes, Scripture records polygamy while the creation pattern to which Jesus points remains the union of the two becoming one flesh.
But there is something even greater you must remember.
Your sexual history is not your identity.
Jesus is not standing over repentant sinners counting bodies.
He is calling people out of darkness and into Himself.
So stop asking only:
“What did I become connected to?”
Start asking:
“Whom do I belong to now?”
If you belong to Christ, then live like someone purchased at immeasurable cost.
If you are married, honor your covenant.
If you are single, honor Christ with your body.
If you are sexually tempted, run toward God instead of negotiating with temptation.
If you have fallen, repent rather than hiding.
If you have been betrayed, know that another person's sin does not reduce your worth.
If you have a past, remember that the Gospel was written for people with pasts.
Just be honest.
Someone reading your three words may realize they are not the only Christian fighting for purity.
It is an invitation to belong completely to Jesus.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but needs grace desperately.
Not because paying for something earns favor with God. It never does.
Scripture never teaches that, and we will not manipulate you by pretending it does.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching reach another person.
And beyond that, stay close because discipleship cannot survive on emotional moments alone.
Jesus is still calling people.
Leave the comment you almost decided not to leave.
Come back to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most important “one flesh” question was never how many people your past connected you to.
Perhaps it was whether your whole life belongs to Christ today.
Your past may explain some of your scars—but it does not get to write the final sentence after Jesus picks up the pen.
